name: Eye color diet
lead: The eye color diet refers to claims that particular foods, supplements, hydration habits or eating patterns can lighten or otherwise change the color of the iris. It appears in wellness content and appearance-focused online discussion as a way to alter eye color without lenses or procedures.

Reference works describe iris color as set mainly by melanin in the iris and by genes such as OCA2 and HERC2 [1][2]. Neither article consulted lists diet as a recognized influence on iris pigmentation, and Grokipedia's article on eye color states that drinking water or hydration does not change iris pigmentation, though hydration may improve the overall look of the eyes [2]. No published clinical study has tested a diet for changing iris color.

paras: Versions of the claim vary: some propose eliminating certain foods, others recommend particular vitamins, herbs or fruit-heavy regimens, with the stated aim of reducing iris melanin or making the eyes appear lighter. The claims are generally presented without a described pathway from dietary intake to iris pigment.

sections.h: What is known about eye color
paras: Iris color depends on melanin quantity and distribution in the stroma and on light scattering. It is polygenic, with HERC2 and OCA2 on chromosome 15 the main known contributors [1][2]. Iris color can shift naturally in infancy, adolescence and adulthood in a minority of people, and some medications (certain prostaglandin analogue drops) can darken irises [1][2]. Sudden changes in adults may accompany conditions such as cataract, glaucoma or iris atrophy [2].
Perceived eye brightness can also vary with factors that do not alter the iris, such as sclera whiteness, redness, lighting and pupil size [2].

No studies found. No published human study has examined whether any diet or supplement changes iris color. Separately, the American Academy of Ophthalmology has warned about procedures and products marketed for changing eye color, such as keratopigmentation, laser depigmentation and certain over-the-counter drops, citing risks including inflammation, raised eye pressure and vision loss [2].

card.summary: Food and supplement routines said to lighten the eyes; iris color is set by melanin and genes and no trial has tested diet.
card.note: No published human studies; no recognized dietary influence on iris pigment.

quick.overview:
The eye color diet is the claim that eating or avoiding certain things can lighten or change your iris color. It is passed around in wellness and appearance communities as a no-procedure route.

Encyclopedia sources attribute iris color to melanin and genes and do not list diet as an influence. No clinical study has tested the idea.
quick.mechanism: Proponents generally propose that diet or supplements reduce iris melanin or brighten the eyes, but no pathway from food to iris pigment has been described in published research. Natural color shifts are linked to development, hormones, medications and disease.
quick.risks: Dietary approaches have no reported direct eye harms in the sources reviewed, though restrictive diets carry their own considerations. Ophthalmology bodies warn against eye-color-changing procedures and drops, and sudden real color change can signal a medical condition.
